definition.text: The development of soil, also called pedogenesis, as shaped by the effects of place, environment and history.

facts.text: It begins with the weathering of freshly accumulated parent material; new soils then deepen through further weathering and deposition, including deposition of dust.
Microbes feed on nutrients released by weathering and produce organic acids and proteins that speed mineral weathering, while their residues help form humus.
Under the Mediterranean climate of Sicily, weathering produces soil at roughly 1/10 mm per year.
As soil develops it supports pioneer species first, then more complex plant and animal communities through ecological succession.
Topsoils deepen as humus from dead plants and microbes accumulates and as organic matter mixes with weathered minerals.
As soils mature, accumulating organic matter, mineral weathering and leaching create layers called horizons that differ in colour, structure, texture and chemistry.
Biogeochemical processes both create and destroy order within soils, and differences in soil-forming factors produce patterns in the distribution of soil types.
Pedogenesis is studied as a branch of pedology; it explains soil distribution today (soil geography) and in past geological periods (paleopedology).

definition.text: The five classic, intertwined influences that govern how a soil develops: parent material, climate, topography, organisms and time.

facts.text: Reordered as climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time, the factors form the acronym CLORPT.
Parent material, the mineral material a soil forms from, turns into soil as it is weathered, transported, deposited and precipitated.
Climate is regarded as the dominant factor; soils show the distinctive characteristics of the climate zones in which they form.
Topography can either hasten or retard the work of climate on a soil.
Each soil has its own combination of microbial, plant, animal and human influences acting on it.
Time acts through the interactions of all the other factors, and how long a profile takes to develop depends strongly on climate, parent material, relief and biota.
The 1938 USDA soil taxonomy divided soils into three orders according to their dominant soil-forming factors.
Intrazonal soils show a local factor of relief or parent material outweighing the zonal effects of climate and vegetation.

definition.text: The influence of climate on soil formation, chiefly through effective precipitation (precipitation minus evapotranspiration) and temperature, which set the rates of chemical, physical and biological processes.

facts.text: When warmth and abundant water coincide in the profile, weathering, leaching and plant growth are all maximized.

Water percolating through the profile carries soluble and suspended material, including clay and dissolved organic matter, from upper layers (eluviation) to lower ones (illuviation), differentiating horizons.
To act, water must penetrate the regolith; the deeper it goes, the deeper the soil is weathered and developed.
In dry regions soluble salts are not leached and may build up enough to curb plant and microbial growth; carbonates and caliche horizons also accumulate.
Colder or drier climates fix less atmospheric carbon as organic matter but also decompose less of it.
Profiles are more distinct in wet, cool climates, where organic matter accumulates, than in wet, warm climates, where it is rapidly consumed.
Climate also acts through vegetation: humid climates favour trees, subhumid and semiarid regions grasses, and arid areas shrubs and brush.
Bare tropical soils under intense evaporation can draw dissolved iron and aluminium upward into a surface hardpan of laterite or bauxite, an irreversible form of degradation.

definition.text: The influence of relief (slope, elevation and aspect) on soil formation through its control of runoff, erosion and the formation of the surface profile.

facts.text: Steep slopes lose soil quickly to erosion and let less rain soak in, so their soils tend to be shallower and less developed than those on nearby level sites.
Soils at the foot of a hill get more water, and slopes facing the sun's path are drier than slopes that do not.
In swales and depressions where runoff collects, the regolith is more deeply weathered and profiles are more advanced.
In the lowest positions saturation restricts drainage and aeration, slowing weathering and decay while speeding the loss of iron and manganese; wetland soils, saline marshes or peat bogs may form.
Recurring topographic patterns produce toposequences or catenas, through differences in erosion, deposition, moisture, plant cover and exposure.
Gravity carries water, solutes and colloids downslope, raising particulate and base content at the foot of hills and mountains.

title: Organisms as a soil-forming factor

definition.text: The influence of plants, animals, fungi, bacteria and humans on how a soil forms.

facts.text: Microorganisms drive key mineral transformations; some bacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen and some fungi extract deep phosphorus and add soil carbon as glomalin.
Plants hold soil against erosion and build humus, and with mycorrhizal fungi and rhizosphere bacteria produce chemicals that break down minerals.
Burrowing macrofauna and mesofauna mix soil and open pores for water and gases, a process called bioturbation.
Mixing by animals, sometimes called pedoturbation, tends to undo the work of the processes that create distinct horizons.
Old burrows in lower horizons often fill with material from the A horizon, leaving features called crotovinas or krotovinas.
Humans, and with them fire, belong to this factor: clearing, tillage, irrigation, fertilizer and lime can abruptly change soil formation.
In the Negev desert, lichen-grazing land snails process between 0.7 and 1.1 metric tons of limestone per hectare per year, starting soil formation.
Nearly half the humus of North American tallgrass-prairie chernozems is charcoal; Neolithic human-set fires are now accepted as helping form chernozems and terra preta.

notes: The section's closing question, whether soil can form without organisms (S:761f522051b3, S:5dffbba9779d), is left to What counts as soil (what-soil-is).

title: Time as a soil-forming factor

definition.text: The span over which the other soil-forming factors interact, which shapes how far a soil has developed.

facts.text: Sand, silt and clay give a soil its texture and their aggregation gives peds, but the development of a distinct B horizon marks a developing soil.
A soil takes from decades to several thousand years to develop a profile, the span depending strongly on climate, parent material, relief and biota.
Fresh flood deposits show no soil development; the old surface is buried and soil formation starts anew in the deposit.
Additions, removals and alterations continue even on stable landscapes, some lasting millions of years, so soils are always subject to new conditions.
The soil life cycle ultimately ends in conditions that leave the soil vulnerable to erosion, though most soil cycles are long.
Time is studied through chronosequences, comparing soils of different ages with small differences in the other factors; paleosols record earlier soil-forming conditions.

contested_note: The notion of soil development toward a mature profile has been criticized, on the grounds that soil is constantly changing as soil-forming factors fluctuate.

definition.text: Vasily Dokuchaev's 1898 equation expressing soil as a function of climate, organisms and parent material over relative time.

facts.text: Dokuchaev, often called the father of pedology, concluded in 1883 that soil forms over time under climate, vegetation, topography and parent material.
The equation reads soil = f(cl, o, p) tr, where tr is relative time: young, mature or old.
Jenny's later state equation differs by treating time as a factor and adding topographic relief.

definition.text: Hans Jenny's 1941 equation treating soil formation as a function of climate, organisms, relief, parent material, time and further open-ended factors: S = f(cl, o, r, p, t, ...).

facts.text: It is often remembered by the mnemonic Clorpt.
Unlike Dokuchaev's equation it treats time as a factor, adds relief, and deliberately leaves room for more state variables as understanding improves.
It can be solved by deduction or empirically; the empirical route, varying one factor while holding the others constant, is the one mostly used today.
That approach produced empirical models of soil formation: climofunctions, biofunctions, topofunctions, lithofunctions and chronofunctions.
Since 1941, soil surveyors worldwide have used it as a qualitative list of the factors behind a region's soil pattern.
Critics hold that the five-factor model, though parsimonious and useful, leaves out the biodynamic processes that produce features such as stonelayers.

definition.text: The removal of soluble materials from one zone of a soil to another by water moving through the profile.

facts.text: It is a soil-forming mechanism distinct from eluviation, which is the loss of mineral and organic colloids rather than dissolved material.
Leached and eluviated materials tend to leave the topsoil and gather in the subsoil, in a horizon called the zone of illuviation.
Laterite, which develops under high temperatures and heavy rainfall, is an example of the process.
In brown podzolic soils leaching washes mobile chemicals out of the A horizon and accumulates iron and aluminium sesquioxides in the B horizon, colouring it rusty orange-brown.
Canadian soil classification marks strongly leached layers as light grey Ae horizons, and in Solonetzic soils progressive leaching moves salts and sodium downward.
Climate directly sets the rate of leaching; it is most intense in warm, humid regions where the soil does not freeze.
Intensive leaching leaves laterite soils less fertile than other soils, and has left reclaimed acid sulfate soils infertile.
Most leaching comes from infiltrating water; it is controlled largely by hydraulic conductivity and described with solute transport models such as Darcy's law.

definition.text: A hydrological model of how irrigation water leaches dissolved substances, notably salt, from soil, depending on the water regime and the soil's properties.

facts.text: It describes the process over time and as a function of the amount of water applied.
Leaching is used to reclaim saline soil or keep irrigated land's salt content favourable, since all irrigation water contains salts.
Leaching curves from the Chacupe pilot area in Peru show deeper-layer salinity first rising with salts from the topsoil, then falling as more water percolates.
Agro-hydro-salinity and leaching models such as SaltMod help determine drainage requirements.

definition.text: A leaching-model parameter that departs from unity where salt is unevenly distributed in the soil or the soil structure is irregular.

facts.text: Soils with low leaching efficiency are hard to reclaim; dense clay in Portugal's Tagus delta measured only 0.10 to 0.15 and was left as coarse pasture.
Clay soil in Egypt's Nile delta has a much better efficiency of 0.7 to 0.8.
The parameter is hard to measure directly and is calibrated by fitting model curves to observed salinity, as with a value of about 0.75 at Mashtul.
Tabulated values range from 0.80 for Tunisian silty clay and 0.70 for illitic clays to between 0.11 and 0.20 for smectitic clays in Peru, Portugal and Thailand.

title: Catena

definition.text: A series of distinct but co-evolving soils arrayed down a slope, all in the same climate and on the same parent material.

facts.text: The concept arose in central Uganda, where chemist W.S. Martin described a hillslope sequence at Bukalasa; Geoffrey Milne coined the term, Latin for chain.
A slope divides into ridge, crest, midslope and toeslope; crests drain freely while toeslopes are wetter, poorly drained and richer in clay and organic matter.
A catena is an open system that forms when climate is uniform along the slope and each facet's inputs and outputs have reached equilibrium, giving a predictable sequence.
Steep middle facets erode faster and are thinner and drier; flatter top and bottom facets carry thicker, deeper soils.
Upper facets lose materials such as salts by eluviation, and lower facets gain them by illuviation.
Easily disaggregated rock and high relief favour distinct soils in source and deposition zones; on low relief, subsurface flow of dissolved and suspended solids dominates.
On acid schists in wet western Scotland a catena runs from peat bog to peaty podzols; on chalk, from brown earths to thin rendzinas and valley fen peat or alluvium.
A mature catena is in equilibrium, with deposition and erosion in balance.

notes: S:be4d0d8d03ed (Milne coined 'catena') is tagged citation needed.

definition.text: The organic-rich, bioturbated upper part of a soil, including the topsoil, where most soil organisms live, reproduce and die.

facts.text: It is mainly a product of organic activity: faunalturbation, floralturbation and fungiturbation mix and destratify the parent material and often sort its particles.
In midlatitude A-E-B-C profiles the biomantle is the part above the B horizon: the A horizon plus any lighter E horizon.
Two-layered biomantles have a basal stonelayer and form in mixed fine and gravelly material; one-layered biomantles form in uniform sands, loess or gravels.
Midlatitude biomantles are often less than 1–2 m thick, while in stable humid tropics, with year-round termites, ants and worms, they are often 5–6 m or more.
As the main zone of bioturbation it is permeable and of low density, speeding percolation through biopores and, above dense subsoils, downslope throughflow.
As originally defined, a biomantle must show at least 50% biofabric, the pelletized fabric made by invertebrates.
In some desert, mountain and freshly eroded bedrock soils the biomantle is the whole soil, with no horizons or weathering zones beneath it.
Australian field practice may simply call the A horizon the biomantle.

title: Biomixing, biotransfer and biosorting
article: Soil biomantle#Three notable bioturbation sub-processes and associated particle comminutions

definition.text: The three overlapping sub-processes of soil bioturbation, which together abrade and reduce particles (particle comminution).

facts.text: Biomixing is the churning done by burrowing vertebrates such as pocket gophers, moles, badgers, wombats, aardvarks and pigs; tree uprooting also matters.
Biotransfer moves soil to the surface or within the biomantle, mainly by 'conveyor-belt' ants, termites and worms; termites may dig many metres for mound-building soil.
In biosorting, burrowers move only particles smaller than their burrows, so larger stones settle and form a stonelayer at the base of the biomantle.
Invertebrates are the main biosorters in tropical soils, while small fossorial vertebrates dominate in many midlatitude deserts, prairies and steppes.

title: Dynamic denudation
article: Soil biomantle#Dynamic denudation, bioturbation and soil biomantle formation

definition.text: The sum of all processes acting in the soil biomantle, in which bioturbation and other organic effects are commonly dominant.

facts.text: The processes include organic matter production, eluviation and illuviation, weathering, erosion and deposition, freeze–thaw, shrink–swell and gravity movements, normally subsidiary to bioturbation.
Plants' role in soil formation is well understood, but animals' role in making soil, horizons, Mima mounds and stone lines was poorly understood until recently.

Wilkinson and Humphreys offer evidence that bioturbation appears to be the most active pedogenic process in many soils; it dominates the upper part of most soils, except possibly vertisols and cryosols.

title: Biomantles and archaeology

definition.text: The finding that most prehistoric cultural materials lie in the soil biomantle, where bioturbation has moved them out of their original context.

facts.text: The exceptions are a few stratified caves and rare open-air sites buried faster than bioturbation could destratify them.
Artifacts wider than burrows, such as cleavers, core-stones and grinding stones, settle downward and join the basal stonelayer.
Smaller flakes are spread through the upper biomantle and turn up in the spoil heaps of gophers, moles and mole-rats.
Since Darwin, the earthworm has been recognized as a key bioturbator of biomantles and artifacts.

related: The Formation of Vegetable Mould Through the Action of Worms

definition.text: A theory of the climatic conditions under which periods of soil formation alternate with periods of soil erosion.

facts.text: Proposed by pedologist Henry Erhart in 1951, it defines two climatic phases: biostasy and rhexistasy.
In biostasy, abundant regular rain under protective vegetation drives chemical alteration, eluviation and illuviation, building eluvial and argillic horizons and sesquioxide-rich subsoils.
In rhexistasy a drier climate thins vegetation, pedogenesis slows, physical weathering dominates, and intense rains erode soils into layers of sand and silt.
Pleistocene glacial periods are considered times of rhexistasy and interglacials times of biostasy.

definition.text: The washing of fine clay from the upper to the lower part of a soil by water moving down through the soil matrix; also called argilluviation.

facts.text: It is the main mechanism forming the clay-enriched argic, or Bt, horizon of Luvisolic soils.
Infiltrating water picks up negatively charged clay as a colloidal suspension and carries it down until a change in conditions makes it flocculate.
Clay settles where water stagnates or meets positive ions deeper down; as it accumulates, pores in the illuvial horizon become finer and trap still more clay.
It is most common in medium-textured loams under moderate to high rainfall, especially beneath deciduous and mixed forests whose organic acids disperse clay.
Very sandy soils drain too fast and lack clay, while clay-rich soils drain so slowly that clay migrates only a short way.
It is widespread in central and eastern Canada, parts of Europe and temperate Asia.
Clay deposited below raises cation exchange capacity, but a thick clay-rich layer can make soils prone to compaction, surface ponding and restricted root growth.
If the clay-enriched layer becomes too compacted, limiting traffic, subsoiling and tile drainage may be needed.

definition.text: An extreme form of leaching that eluviates iron and aluminium sesquioxides from the upper soil.

facts.text: It generally occurs where precipitation is greater than evapotranspiration.
Decaying organic matter releases organic acids that act as chelating agents; under conifers, a thin litter layer yields acidic mor humus (pH 4.5) rich in them.
Chelating agents break down clay and release iron and aluminium, which become sesquioxides and move from the A horizon down to the B horizon.
Bases such as calcium and potassium are leached too, leaving quartz and silica in a light, eluviated AE horizon at the base of the A horizon.
The B horizon has a dark layer of illuviated organic matter and bases over a red-orange layer of iron and aluminium sesquioxides.
Waterlogging above the B horizon can saturate the A horizon, producing mottling or a gleyed podzol.
It is especially intense in boreal and cool temperate pine forests, whose litter is rich in phenolic compounds and fulvic acid; tropical forests show little or none.

definition.text: The process in which metal ions in the upper soil bind with organic ligands into chelates that move downward by eluviation and are then deposited.

facts.text: Iron, aluminium, manganese, calcium, magnesium and trace elements can be chelated, mostly by ligands from soil organic matter.
Fulvic acid–metal chelates leach and deposit strongly, typically producing a grey-white leached layer above a dark brown or red deposition layer.
Iron and aluminium move easily at low pH and under reducing conditions, but precipitate as pH rises (around 7–8) or under oxidizing conditions.
Clay adsorbs chelates and weakens their leaching, while coarse-textured or water-saturated soils enhance it.

title: Chronosequence

definition.text: A set of sites that share similar attributes but differ in age, used to study change over time.

facts.text: In soil science it is a group of sites that have developed for different lengths of time with small differences in other soil-forming factors, used to assess time as a factor.
It assumes nothing but age differs between sites; because this often cannot be tested, its use in field successional studies has been debated.
It lets slow processes such as forest development, which take decades or centuries, be studied from field data gathered in a few months.
A classic use is tracing plant and microbial succession on recently deglaciated ground; a 2005 study used distance from a glacier's nose as a proxy for site age.
Along a chronosequence, a cambic horizon develops into an argillic (Bt) horizon once the soil becomes an alfisol.

contested_note: Because the assumption that only age differs between sites often cannot be tested, the use of chronosequences in field successional studies has been debated.

definition.text: The variation of soil properties within an area, usually expressed through soil classes.

facts.text: Studies began with soil series–area relationships (Beckett and Bie, 1978); McBratney developed the term in 1992 while discussing landscape preservation.
Ibáñez and colleagues (1995) first applied ecological diversity indices—richness, relative abundance and the Shannon index—treating soil classes as taxa.
It measures soil variation, is a function of soil formation, and is used to analyse soil spatial patterns, soil geography and pedogenetic theories.
In eastern North Carolina and the Ouachita Mountains, variability within plots, tied to individual trees and local lithology, outweighed differences between plots.
A 2003 US study found the West richest in soil taxa and, at the series level, taxa increasing steadily with area, indicating considerable soil endemism.
Conventional indices ignore how similar soil classes are; the mean soil taxonomic distance, which accounts for it, has been shown to be a better measure.
Knowing natural pedodiversity helps preserve the soil cover and rebuild quasi-natural soil systems on degraded land.

title: Laterite

definition.text: A soil type rich in iron and aluminium that often forms in hot, wet areas, mostly in the tropics.

facts.text: Nearly all laterites are rusty red because of their high iron oxide content.
Francis Buchanan-Hamilton named a laterite formation in southern India in 1807, from Latin later, brick, because the compact soil cuts easily into building blocks.
Yves Tardy calculated that laterites cover about one-third of Earth's continental land, including most land between the tropics of Cancer and Capricorn.
Laterite covers are thick on stable shields and cratons; the cap on a plateau in Madhya Pradesh, India, is 30 m thick.
Laterites outside today's humid tropics formed when the land lay near the equator, and are read as signs of climatic change, continental drift or both.
The term has been applied to cemented sesquioxide-rich horizons, any reddish surface soil, a rock type and whole weathering profiles.
Laterites may contain pisolites and ferricrete, and relief inversion can leave them in elevated positions.

contested_note: Because 'laterite' has been used for a soil, a rock, a weathering profile and even a theory of weathering, researchers such as Paton, Williams and Ollier call the usage confused and some urge abandoning the term.
notes: Contested note rests on S:7b34828d0b50, S:660ab5c1d7a9 and S:136bd11007e6.

title: Laterization

definition.text: The prolonged chemical weathering of rock under tropical conditions that produces laterite.

facts.text: It needs high temperatures and heavy rainfall alternating with dry seasons: rain leaches the rock, then capillary action lifts the dissolved ions to the surface in the dry season.
Acid dissolves the host minerals, hydrolysis precipitates insoluble iron and aluminium oxides, and sodium, potassium, calcium and magnesium are leached away.
Solutions of the right pH dissolve silica in preference to aluminium and iron oxides, leaving mainly iron and aluminium behind.
The first products are kaolinized rocks called saprolites; quartz is the most abundant mineral surviving from the parent rock.
Gentle crests and plateaus favour it by protecting the weathered cover from erosion.
It was most active from the mid-Tertiary to the mid-Quaternary (35 to 1.5 million years ago), slowed with abrupt global cooling, and continues today at a reduced rate.
Mafic, iron-rich rocks yield iron oxides, granitic iron-poor rocks yield bauxites, and ultramafic rocks yield nickel laterites.

notes: Kept separate from Ferrallitisation: the sources describe them on different pages, and laterite needs alternating wet and dry seasons while ferrallitic soils form under year-round rain.

definition.text: The agricultural behaviour of laterite soils, which are clay-rich but heavily leached.

facts.text: High clay gives them more cation exchange capacity, plasticity and water-holding capacity but lower permeability than sandy soils, so rain enters slowly.
Intensive leaching leaves them less fertile than other soils, but they respond readily to manure and irrigation and suit plantation crops such as oil palm, tea, coffee and cashew.
If their structure degrades, a hard surface crust forms that blocks infiltration and seedling emergence and increases runoff.
'Bio-reclamation of degraded lands', using planting pits, residues and drought-tolerant crops, has rehabilitated degraded laterite soils in Niger.

definition.text: Laterite cut into blocks while moist and soft, which then harden on exposure to air into a durable building material.

facts.text: It is mined below the water table while wet and soft; as moisture evaporates, iron compounds lock into a rigid lattice that resists the weather.
Khmer builders used laterite with sandstone in the Angkor monuments, including the foundations and inner parts of Angkor Wat behind its sandstone face.
After 1000 AD Angkorian construction shifted to rectangular temple enclosures of laterite, brick and stone.
Since the mid-1970s laterite has replaced stone as a road base course in trials; Malawi saved US$40,000 per km this way in 1984.

definition.text: Thick, porous and slightly permeable laterite layers that hold and yield groundwater, especially in rural tropical areas.

facts.text: Tropical bedrock is often impermeable granite, gneiss, schist or sandstone, so the laterite above it becomes the usable aquifer.
Sri Lanka's Southwestern Laterite (Cabook) Aquifer recharges rapidly with the April–May rains and the monsoon, and supports shallow dug wells.
In some dense suburbs its water table can fall to 15 m below ground after more than 65 dry days.

definition.text: The use of iron- and aluminium-rich laterite to remove phosphorus and heavy metals from wastewater.

facts.text: In Northern Ireland, where farm phosphorus enriches lakes, local laterite, a low-grade bauxite, is used in acid solution followed by precipitation at sewage works.
Laboratory tests removed 99% of phosphorus from solution, and a pilot-scale facility 96%.
Percolating laterite columns lowered cadmium, chromium and lead to undetectable concentrations.

title: Lateritic ores

definition.text: Metal ores concentrated in laterites, including aluminium, iron, manganese, nickel, copper and gold.

facts.text: Aluminium is found in bauxites, iron and manganese in iron-rich hard crusts, nickel and copper in disintegrated rock, and gold in mottled clays.
Bauxite, the main aluminium ore, is a variety of laterite averaging 45 to 60% Al2O3 and 20 to 30% Fe2O3 by weight, mainly gibbsite in newer tropical deposits.
About 70% of Earth's land-based nickel resources lie in laterites, which currently supply about 40% of world nickel production.
Northern Ireland's basaltic laterites, up to 30 m thick, were once a major source of iron and aluminium ore.

notes: Nickel share: S:39843177db10 says about 40% currently; S:20191bea87d0 gives 42% in 2003 and an expected 51% by 2012. Different years, so not recorded as a conflict.

definition.text: An ancient soil that formed in the past.

facts.text: In geology it is a former soil buried under sediments such as alluvium or loess, or under lava or volcanic ash, and in older deposits lithified into rock.
In soil science it is a soil formed long ago whose properties bear no relation to today's climate or vegetation, found on old cratons and outliers of ancient rock.
The record reaches into the Precambrian, with rare paleosols older than 2.5 billion years.
Over the last 50 million years drying climates hardened former tropical soils across much of Australia into crusts so unweatherable that only poorly developed soils form on them.
Such relict soils are exceedingly infertile, with available phosphorus orders of magnitude lower than in younger temperate soils, yet often hold exceptional biodiversity.
Pollen, phytoliths, carbon isotopes and leaf waxes in paleosols reveal past plant life, including the balance of C3 and C4 plants.
Glacial loess layers separated by paleosols record glaciations, and stacked paleosol sequences are useful in paleoseismology.

title: Paleosol identification

definition.text: The recognition of a fossil or buried soil from criteria such as formation in place on bedrock and up-profile changes consistent with weathering.

facts.text: Rye and Holland (1998) set out five criteria, prompted by Precambrian paleosols but applicable to paleosols of any age.
They include formation in situ on bedrock, soft-sediment deformation at the top of the profile, and up-profile changes in chemistry, texture and mineralogy matching terrestrial weathering.
Field signs include horizonation, bedrock corestones within finer overlying material, and traces of surface processes such as roots, burrows, organic matter and redox alteration.
Diagnostic horizons and features separate paleosol types; all have an A horizon, but histosols also have an O horizon above it.

notes: The crawled criteria list keeps only three of Rye and Holland's five criteria.

definition.text: The naming of paleosols, which mostly borrows the orders of USDA soil taxonomy because modern systems fit ancient soils poorly.

facts.text: Geology, life and the atmosphere changed greatly over the paleosol record, notably at the Great Oxidation Event 2.42 billion years ago, so modern classification fits poorly.
An alfisol, a forest soil, could not exist before trees, and it is defined by chemical properties not preserved in rock.
A paleosol-specific naming scheme has been proposed but is used only sporadically.
The USDA hierarchy cannot be applied to paleosols below the order level.

definition.text: The use of paleosols to gauge the climate they formed in, since rates and styles of weathering depend on climate.

facts.text: Mean annual precipitation and mean annual air temperature are the most commonly reconstructed variables.
Many proxies rely on chemical changes through the profile during weathering, burial and post-burial alteration, and not every proxy suits every paleosol.
Most proxies work only for Phanerozoic paleosols, as landscape processes changed sharply after land plants arose.
Seasonality proxies rely on pedogenic carbonate formed as soils wet and dry, and are still being tested and refined.

definition.text: The use of paleosol chemistry to infer the past composition of the atmosphere, with which soils form in near-constant contact.

facts.text: The oxidation of paleosols has served as an indicator of atmospheric oxygen, which has risen over Earth's history.
Atmospheric carbon dioxide has been reconstructed from soil gas exchange, carbon isotopes in pedogenic carbonate nodules and multi-gas mass balances.
These methods are being actively developed in early-Earth research.

title: Polygenetic soil

definition.text: A soil, such as a paleosol, that shows evidence of continued soil development under later conditions.

facts.text: Most soils are polygenetic, so a younger pedogenic signal may overprint, mask or erase an older one.
Paleosols and polygenetic soils with paleo-argillic horizons include the Wounded Moose paleosol of the Yukon and the Berino Paleosol of New Mexico.
Terra rossa has been proposed to be polygenetic, its altered parent material including volcanic ash, non-carbonate and aeolian sediments.

notes: No article; passes the 2+ pages test (Argillic, Soil memory, Terra rossa (soil)).

definition.text: The idea that soil keeps a record of past natural changes, environmental conditions and human activity.

facts.text: Nikiforoff coined the term in 1953, echoing Dokuchaev's dictum that soil is 'a mirror of the landscape'.
Soils store records palimpsest-wise (pedomemory), with successive features overprinting each other, while layered sediments store them book-wise (lithomemory), in datable order.
It is used to study climate change, land-use history and archaeological evidence; persistent environmental DNA in cultivated soils is read as a 'memory effect'.
Because most soils are polygenetic, the record is partial and 'censored', and equifinality complicates reading it, so the concept serves as an exploratory tool.

definition.text: The ability of soil microbial communities to change their structure, diversity and activity in response to natural or human factors and to keep those changes over time.

facts.text: Many bacteria survive in dormant states for long periods, persisting through large environmental changes.
PCR and next-generation sequencing characterize soil bacterial communities from their DNA, well suited to detecting traces of past influences.
Distinctive bacterial communities mark an Iron Age settlement in Sicily, Iron Age cremation burials, medieval activity areas and Neolithic ditch infills.

definition.text: The mixing of material between soil horizons, an important factor in soil formation.

facts.text: It includes the churning of clays, cryoturbation and bioturbation.
It transforms soils through destratification, mixing and sorting, and creates preferential flow paths for soil gas and infiltrating water.
Mixing by animals tends to counteract the processes that create distinct horizons.
Precipitation of surface salts disrupts soils locally but is not counted as pedoturbation because it does not mix horizons.
With weathering and humification, pedoturbation by animals is a main process in forming oxisols.
It belongs to perturbation, the wider set of pedological and sedimentary processes that change water-borne alluvial sediments and in situ soils over time.

definition.text: The process by which rock is changed into a soil of kaolinite clay and sesquioxides, the hydrated oxides of iron and aluminium.

facts.text: In humid tropics with consistently high temperatures and rainfall, chemical weathering breaks rock down rapidly into clays, which later break down further to form silica.
The silica is leached away while iron and aluminium sesquioxides remain, giving many tropical soils their characteristic red colour.
It is the reverse of podsolisation, in which silica remains and iron and aluminium are removed.
Year-round rain in tropical rainforests produces ferrallitic soils, while savannas with alternating wet and dry seasons have ferruginous soils.

title: Sewage treatment

definition.text: Wastewater treatment that removes contaminants from sewage so the effluent can be discharged or reused without polluting water.

facts.text: It usually involves primary and secondary treatment, and advanced plants add a tertiary polishing stage.
Sewage can be treated close to where it is produced, in decentralized or on-site systems such as septic tanks.
Locally available laterite has been used at sewage treatment works to remove phosphorus and heavy metals.

notes: Assigned to this chapter by the concept graph, apparently through Laterite's wastewater use. It is wastewater engineering, not soil formation, so it is drafted only for the record and excluded; if the course needs it, it belongs with Contamination and remediation or Septic drain field.

title: Stonelayer

definition.text: A subsurface soil layer dominated by particles coarser than 2 mm that generally mimics the surface topography; also called a stone line.

facts.text: It forms the basal horizon of two-layered soil biomantles.
One stone thick it shows in a pit as a 'stone line'; several stones thick it is a 'stone zone'.
Its gravel may be quartzose rock fragments, iron–manganese nodules, artifacts, shells or precious stones; where present it often acts as a subsurface drain or even an aquifer.
Stone lines in soils follow the surface and are non-imbricated, pointing to a pedogenic origin; water-laid stone lines in sediments are imbricated and geogenic.

notes: Merges the assigned pages Stonelayer and Stone line, which describe the same feature.

title: Stone-line origin debate

definition.text: The long controversy over whether stonelayers in soils formed by geological processes or by soil-forming, largely biological, processes.

facts.text: Few Earth-science topics have caused more controversy, spanning archaeology, geology, geomorphology, ecology and pedology on every continent but Antarctica.
Sharpe coined 'stone-line' in 1938 from South Carolina, reading it as abiotic mass transfer on slopes, unaware of earlier names and drawings, including Darwin's.
It has been read as glacial evidence and as an eroded pavement buried under tropical loess, while Morrás and colleagues (2009) argue it is the base of soil biomantles.
Whether an interpreter favours a geogenic or pedogenic origin often reflects their background and training.

contested_note: Stonelayers have been interpreted as geogenic (glacial deposits, erosional lags, buried pavements) or as pedogenic products of biomantle bioturbation, and the literature remains divided.

definition.text: An oxide with two atoms of an element for every three of oxygen, such as the iron and aluminium oxides Fe2O3 and Al2O3.

facts.text: Many contain a metal in the +3 oxidation state; in soil, the sesquioxides that matter are those of iron and aluminium.
Podsolisation washes iron and aluminium sesquioxides out of the A horizon down to the B horizon, where they build a red-orange layer.
In ferrallitisation silica is leached away while sesquioxides stay behind, giving many tropical soils their red colour; laterite names sesquioxide-rich horizons.
Horizon notation marks their build-up with suffixes: s for illuvial and o for residual sesquioxide accumulation.

definition.text: The rate at which bedrock weathers into soil, expressed as a function of soil thickness.

facts.text: A general model has bedrock weathering decline exponentially with soil thickness h, as de/dt = P0 exp(−kh), where P0 is the maximum weathering rate and k an empirical constant.
Weathering slows under thicker soil because temperature swings and average water penetration both fall off exponentially with depth.
P0 ranged from 0.08 to 2.0 mm/yr at northern California sites and 0.05–0.14 mm/yr in southeastern Australia, while k varied little, from 2 to 4 m−1; both depend on climate and parent material.
The older humped model, from G.K. Gilbert in 1877, has weathering fastest under an intermediate soil thickness, since bare rock sheds the water that chemical weathering needs.

definition.text: Soil mixing caused by the shrinking and swelling of smectite clays, sometimes called self-mulching.

facts.text: Specific to vertisolic soils, it is driven by wetting–drying cycles and needs at least 30% clay.
It opens vertical cracks up to 2 centimetres wide and 50 centimetres or more deep, which fill with sloughed-in surface material.
It can blend horizons until they are hard to tell apart, and produces gilgai topography and slickensides.
Such soils are very productive when irrigated but hard to plough and manage.

definition.text: A bowl-shaped pit in the subsoil made by a tree, through long root growth or when a toppled tree tears out its rootwad.

facts.text: The pit can be several meters across and 1–2 metres deep, and exposes humus-poor, mineral-rich soil.
Tree throw drives bedrock weathering and soil formation, fastest in soils of intermediate thickness; under soils deeper than roots, no bedrock is upturned.
Before trees appeared about 370 million years ago, bedrock weathering was too slow to keep thick soils on hilly terrain.
Tree-throw pits and the mounds of rotting fallen trees form the pit-and-mound topography of old-growth forest.

definition.text: The change in species composition of an ecological community over time.

facts.text: Primary succession colonizes new surfaces with no life, such as bare rock, lava flows or freshly exposed till; secondary succession follows a disturbance.
Pioneers such as microorganisms, lichens and mosses come first, followed by grasses, shrubs and trees.
Plants change the soil as they grow, adding organic matter to litter and humus, altering nutrients and pH and allowing soil formation.
Soil properties and nutrient cycles are shaped by the community and in turn steer further succession.

definition.text: The geomorphic processes that result from seasonal freezing and thawing, very often in areas of permafrost.

facts.text: Periglacial environments are anywhere freezing and thawing significantly modify the landscape, not only at the edges of former glaciers.
About a quarter of Earth's land has periglacial conditions now, and another quarter or fifth had them during the Pleistocene.
Frost heaving, solifluction and ice-wedge formation are its hallmark processes.
Walery Łoziński introduced the term in 1909.

definition.text: The soil-forming factors work through four groups of processes: additions, losses, transformations and translocations.

facts.text: Additions include organic matter, fertilizers, dust deposition and other mineral soil arriving at a soil.
Losses are soil moved away by wind or water, or chemical compounds leached, eroded or harvested from it.
Transformations are the chemical or physical weathering of soil particles or components.
Translocations are the movement of organic or mineral soil components between horizons within a profile.
These processes distinguish soils from layers of material laid down by geologic processes, and how far they have gone helps tell soils apart.
Transfers include eluviation, which removes material from a horizon, and illuviation, which deposits it; clay, and iron and aluminium organic complexes, move down with soil water.
Mixing, or turbation, is also a transfer, caused by organisms or by physical agents such as clay shrink-swell and freeze-thaw.
Weathering releases ions from minerals or turns them into secondary minerals, which may reform deeper in the soil; ions lost altogether are leached.

definition.text: The named positions along a hillslope, from summit to toeslope, each with its own shape and role in moving soil material.

facts.text: The summit is the level top of an upland feature and the shoulder is the convex, erosional edge leading to the backslope.
The backslope is the steepest part, shaped mainly by mass wasting and running water.
The footslope is gently inclined and concave, where colluvium and alluvium accumulate, and the toeslope is a constructional surface where alluvium collects.
A stream terrace is a level strip of an abandoned flood plain, and a flood plain is built of sediment deposited during floods.

definition.text: Precipitation and temperature together decide how much water moves down through a soil and how strongly it is leached.

facts.text: Leaching moves soluble salts down the profile and can carry suspended clay into the subsoil; more precipitation leaches them deeper.
Leaching lowers pH, removes basic cations (Ca2+, Mg2+, K+, Na+) and lowers nutrient content, so desert soils are little leached and humid forest soils extensively.
Higher temperature raises evapotranspiration, so with equal rainfall the cooler region has more effective precipitation and more highly leached soils.
In the Northern Hemisphere, north-facing slopes get less direct sun and so tend to be more weathered, deeper and more leached than warmer, drier south-facing ones.

definition.text: How a soil's horizons, chemistry and productivity change as it ages from parent material to old soil.

facts.text: Parent material has no horizons, a young soil (about 10 to 1,000 years) a slight profile, a mature soil (1,000 to 10,000 years) a well-developed one and an old soil (10,000 to 100,000 years) an extensive one.
Typical profiles run C R, then A C R, then O A Bt C R, then O A E Bs C R as the soil ages.

In a young soil humus accumulates and carbonates leach; in a mature soil humus peaks and clays leach, with maximum illuviation; in an old soil humus declines, carbonates are gone and the surface is very acidic.
Crop productivity is low to moderate in young soil, good in young-to-mature, maximal in mature and low in old soil.
Once vegetation grew, nitrogen entered from rain and from lichens, algae and legumes, organic matter built up a dark A horizon, and rain leached calcium and magnesium carbonates.
Where soils stay highly calcareous the lime limits clay leaching, slowing profile development; on permeable material, clay moved from the A into the B and formed an argillic horizon.

definition.text: A field method that estimates surface runoff from percent slope and the texture of the surface horizon.

facts.text: Percent slope is rise over run times 100, read directly with an Abney level or clinometer held parallel to the slope.
Runoff rises with slope and falls with infiltration rate, and soil erosion generally rises as runoff increases.
Granular, porous soils shed less water than massive, low-porosity soils because more water infiltrates.
Plant cover intercepts raindrops and reduces erosion, while a moister soil saturates sooner and so runs off sooner.
In the table, slopes of 0-1% give very slow runoff for all textures, 6-12% gives rapid runoff for loams but very rapid for clays, and over 18% is very rapid for all textures.

title: Human activity as a soil-forming factor

definition.text: Human use transforms soils, mainly through land conversion, erosion, mining and construction.

facts.text: Converting forest or grassland to cropland usually lowers soil organic matter; globally about 30% of the original soil organic carbon is lost.
Erosion removes the organically enriched surface layer, losing the most fertile soil and sometimes exposing a growth-limiting layer such as a high-sodium one.
Deposited eroded soil over-thickens lower slopes, burying the original topsoil under less fertile subsoil to give a cumulic soil.
Soils heavily disrupted by people, as by mining or pipelines, are termed anthropogenic; reconstructed soils inevitably differ from the original profile.
